											173 text Even objects with no net charge can be attracted to charged objects through a process called polarization. In polarization, the charges within a neutral object rearrange slightly—positive and negative charges shift in opposite directions—creating a temporary attraction. This effect is especially noticeable in insulators, where the charges can't move freely but can still shift within molecules.
											174 heading Polarization and Its Effects, Value: 2
												175 text Polarization and Its Effects
											176 text Explore how polarization occurs and its effects in different materials and scenarios. Polarization is the process by which the distribution of charges within an object is altered, often resulting in temporary attraction between objects, even if they remain electrically neutral overall.

												191 text Why Do Charges Gather at Sharp Points?
											192 text On conductors, excess charge tends to concentrate at sharp points or edges, creating very strong electric fields in those areas. This can lead to electrostatic discharge, where charge suddenly jumps through the air as a spark. Lightning rods use this principle to safely direct electric charge from the atmosphere to the ground, protecting buildings from lightning strikes.
